claims.statement: Data bus inversion reduces the number of simultaneously switching outputs on an LPDDR5X data byte.
claims.source: JESD209-5x, DBI mode definitions
claims.conditions: Per byte lane, DBI enabled
claims.note: Wording now distinguishes transition-minimising from level-minimising inversion and claims no universal 50% bound.

claims.statement: LPDDR5X reaches 8533 MT/s.
claims.source: JEDEC press release, "JEDEC Updates Standard for Low Power Memory Devices: LPDDR5"
claims.conditions: A specific edition and speed bin
claims.note: JEDEC’s own announcement of JESD209-5B states the speed extension to 8533 Mbps. Verifies that the family reaches this rate; says nothing about which speed bin a given part supports, or about the electricals. JESD209-5C (July 2023) is the current revision and is downloadable from jedec.org after registration.
claims.source_title: JEDEC — LPDDR5 standard update announcement

claims.statement: LPDDR5 reaches 6400 MT/s.
claims.source: JEDEC press release, "JEDEC Updates Standard for Low Power Memory Devices: LPDDR5"
claims.conditions: A specific edition and speed bin
claims.note: The same announcement gives 6400 Mbps as the previous revision’s ceiling, which is the LPDDR5 figure. Verifies the rate, not any particular device’s bin.
claims.source_title: JEDEC — LPDDR5 standard update announcement

claims.statement: An LPDDR5X channel is normally point-to-point, controller to DRAM, with no connector and no fly-by topology — but a dual-rank or two-die configuration puts more than one device on the same data net.
claims.source: Synopsys LPDDR5 technical bulletin and LPDDR5X/5/4X controller documentation, on rank and dual-channel support; byte-mode descriptions of two 8-bit dies on one 16-bit channel
claims.conditions: Single-rank, single-die is the common case; rank count and byte mode change the loading
claims.note: Corrected. "Point to point rather than multidrop" was too strong: LPDDR5 defines non-target ODT precisely because a dual-rank configuration exists, and a device may be built as two 8-bit dies sharing one 16-bit channel. The page already says so — it calls "never multi-drop" a step too far and tells the reader to check the configuration — so this row now matches what the page claims rather than what it used to.
claims.source_title: Synopsys — Key features designers should know about LPDDR5

claims.statement: WCK is the write data clock on LPDDR5X.
claims.source: Synopsys LPDDR5 technical bulletin, on the WCK and RDQS forwarded clocks
claims.conditions: LPDDR5 and its LPDDR5X extension; WCK runs at two or four times the command clock
claims.note: Confirmed: LPDDR5 introduces two unidirectional strobes, WCK for writes and RDQS for reads, with WCK forwarded at two or four times the CK rate. Scoped rather than verified because the ratio options and their training are in JESD209-5, which has not been read.
claims.source_title: Synopsys — Key features designers should know about LPDDR5

claims.statement: Read and write training centre the strobe in the data eye.
claims.source: JESD209-5x training sequences
claims.conditions: The training steps a controller actually runs
claims.note: Narrowed: training also adjusts ODT, drive strength and reference levels, so 'training centres the eye' is one of several things it does. The panel labels its training model illustrative.

claims.statement: A PCIe Gen 4 channel insertion loss budget is about 28 dB at 8 GHz.
claims.source: Texas Instruments SNLA426, high-speed PCB layout for PCIe Gen 5; Astera Labs in Electronic Design, on managing the PCIe 5.0 channel insertion loss budget
claims.conditions: At the Nyquist frequency of the data rate: 8 GHz for 16 GT/s
claims.note: The number is only meaningful with its frequency, and the sources supply it: 28 dB at 8 GHz for Gen 4. Independent design guidance agrees on the figure. Scoped rather than verified because the reference PLANE — what the budget is measured between — is defined in the Base and CEM specifications, and that is what decides whether a given measurement can be compared with it.
claims.source_title: Texas Instruments SNLA426 — High-speed PCB layout for PCIe Gen 5

claims.statement: A PCIe Gen 5 channel insertion loss budget is about 36 dB at 16 GHz.
claims.source: Texas Instruments SNLA426, high-speed PCB layout for PCIe Gen 5; Astera Labs in Electronic Design, on managing the PCIe 5.0 channel insertion loss budget
claims.conditions: At the Nyquist frequency of the data rate: 16 GHz for 32 GT/s
claims.note: The number is only meaningful with its frequency, and the sources supply it: 36 dB at 16 GHz for Gen 5. Independent design guidance agrees on the figure. Scoped rather than verified because the reference PLANE — what the budget is measured between — is defined in the Base and CEM specifications, and that is what decides whether a given measurement can be compared with it.
claims.source_title: Texas Instruments SNLA426 — High-speed PCB layout for PCIe Gen 5

claims.statement: Gen 5 designs commonly backdrill long via stubs.
claims.source: none — channel-dependent practice
claims.conditions: Stub length relative to the Nyquist quarter-wave
claims.note: Treated as an implementation remedy, never a specification requirement.

claims.statement: PCIe 6.0 uses FLIT mode.
claims.source: Synopsys, "PCIe 6.0 Verification of FEC and CRC"; Cadence PCIe 6.0 electrical testing white paper
claims.conditions: All rates once negotiated
claims.note: IP vendors implementing the specification describe the 256-byte FLIT carrying TLP payload, an 8-byte CRC and a 6-byte FEC, with a lightweight single-symbol-correcting FEC backed by CRC and replay. That supports FLIT mode as a mechanism. The normative requirement and its exact field layout need the Base specification.
claims.source_title: Synopsys — PCIe 6.0 verification of FEC and CRC

claims.statement: PCIe 6.0 applies forward error correction.
claims.source: Synopsys, "PCIe 6.0 Verification of FEC and CRC"; Cadence PCIe 6.0 electrical testing white paper
claims.conditions: Per FLIT
claims.note: IP vendors implementing the specification describe the 256-byte FLIT carrying TLP payload, an 8-byte CRC and a 6-byte FEC, with a lightweight single-symbol-correcting FEC backed by CRC and replay. That supports forward error correction as a mechanism. The normative requirement and its exact field layout need the Base specification.
claims.source_title: Synopsys — PCIe 6.0 verification of FEC and CRC

claims.statement: PCIe 6.0 applies a CRC with link-level replay.
claims.source: Synopsys, "PCIe 6.0 Verification of FEC and CRC"; Cadence PCIe 6.0 electrical testing white paper
claims.conditions: Per FLIT
claims.note: IP vendors implementing the specification describe the 256-byte FLIT carrying TLP payload, an 8-byte CRC and a 6-byte FEC, with a lightweight single-symbol-correcting FEC backed by CRC and replay. That supports a CRC with link-level replay as a mechanism. The normative requirement and its exact field layout need the Base specification.
claims.source_title: Synopsys — PCIe 6.0 verification of FEC and CRC

claims.statement: A PCIe 6.0 FLIT is 256 bytes: 236 of transaction-layer data, 6 of data-link information, 8 of CRC and 6 of FEC.
claims.source: PCI-SIG PCI Express Base Specification 6.0, FLIT mode
claims.conditions: FLIT mode, as defined in Base 6.0; later revisions may differ
claims.note: The page states this as a vendor description and labels it unchecked. The byte split appears consistently in vendor material, but the normative layout is in the Base specification, which has not been read.

claims.statement: PCIe 6.0 tolerates a raw error rate near 1e-6 and delivers about 1e-12 after correction.
claims.source: Cadence PCIe 6.0 electrical testing white paper; PCI-SIG figures as reported by EDA and test vendors
claims.conditions: Which metric — BER, FLIT error rate, or post-FEC — must be named
claims.note: The 1e-6 raw and 1e-12 delivered figures are consistently reported as the PAM4 versus NRZ framing behind the FEC decision. Reported by implementers rather than read from the specification, so the page presents them as the design intent and not as a requirement.
claims.source_title: Cadence — PCIe 6.0 electrical testing for high data bandwidth applications

claims.statement: A Gen 6-capable link uses FLIT mode at lower rates as well.
claims.source: Cadence, "Unravelling PCIe 6.0 FLIT mode challenges"; Synopsys PCIe 6.0 design material
claims.conditions: FLIT support is advertised during Polling and Configuration; once negotiated it applies at every rate
claims.note: Confirmed with the mechanism behind it: 256-byte FLITs are supported at 2.5, 5, 8, 16 and 32 GT/s for backward compatibility, negotiation happens through the FLIT Mode Supported bit in the TS1 Data Rate Identifier during link training, and once enabled a speed change to a lower rate stays in FLIT mode. IP vendors implementing it, not the Base text.
claims.source_title: Cadence — Unravelling PCIe 6.0 FLIT mode challenges

claims.statement: PCIe Gen 4 and Gen 5 define eleven transmitter presets, P0 to P10.
claims.source: Tektronix, "10 Things to Know about PCIe"; Synopsys PCIe 5.0 technical bulletin
claims.conditions: Per edition; the preset table is edition-specific
claims.note: Vendor test and IP documentation consistently gives eleven transmitter presets, P0 to P10, for Gen 3 onwards. The preset TABLE — the preshoot and de-emphasis each one defines — is in the Base specification and has not been read, so the page states the count and the mechanism, not the values.
claims.source_title: Tektronix — 10 Things to Know about PCIe

claims.statement: The PAM4 links in common use pair it with forward error correction.
claims.source: would need the standards set defined and each one checked
claims.conditions: 'In common use' is doing the work here
claims.note: Narrowed from 'PAM4 standards mandate FEC', which would need every such standard read.

claims.statement: MIPI M-PHY v5.0 defines HS-GEAR5.
claims.source: MIPI press release, M-PHY v5.0
claims.conditions: The announcement names the gear; the electricals are in the specification
claims.note: Public fact from the standards body's own announcement. Verifies the existence of the gear and nothing about its electricals.
claims.source_title: MIPI Alliance — M-PHY v5.0 announcement

claims.statement: M-PHY HS-GEAR5 runs at 23.32 Gb/s per lane.
claims.source: MIPI press release, M-PHY v5.0
claims.conditions: Raw lane rate, before 128b/132b encoding overhead
claims.note: The page said 23.2 Gb/s; the announcement says 23.32. Neither figure is wrong for a different quantity — raw versus post-encoding differ — so the page now states the raw rate and names it as raw. The discrepancy is why this is split from C-12a.
claims.source_title: MIPI Alliance — M-PHY v5.0 announcement

claims.statement: UFS 4.0 binds M-PHY HS-GEAR5.
claims.source: JESD220E and the M-PHY revision it references
claims.conditions: Which M-PHY revision UFS 4.0 cites
claims.note: MIPI’s own announcement establishes that M-PHY v5.0 defines HS-GEAR5 at 23.32 Gbps (recorded separately as C-12a). What needs JESD220E is the BINDING — that UFS 4.0 requires that gear rather than merely permitting it. Note also that JEDEC published UFS 5.0 (JESD220H) in February 2026 on M-PHY 6.0 with HS-G6, so the page should say which generation it describes.

claims.statement: UFS over M-PHY uses spread-spectrum clocking.
claims.source: MIPI M-PHY
claims.conditions: Whether it is required or optional, and its profile
claims.note: Spread-spectrum clocking is described in M-PHY material as an option for EMI control, and the page should say optional rather than used. What needs the specification is whether UFS mandates it and with what modulation limits.

claims.statement: An M-PHY burst requires re-acquisition from a preamble.
claims.source: Mixel, "M-PHY benefits and challenges"; Synopsys M-PHY article, on HS-BURST structure and STALL
claims.conditions: HS-MODE; STALL is the power-saving state between bursts
claims.note: Confirmed by the burst structure: an HS-BURST is PREPARE, SYNC, MARKERs and then data, where SYNC is the symbol sequence the receiver uses to bit-synchronise to the embedded clock. Between bursts the lane sits in STALL with activity stopped, so each burst re-acquires. That is the mechanism the page describes.
claims.source_title: Mixel — M-PHY benefits and challenges

claims.statement: USB 3.2 spread-spectrum clocking is down-spread, 0 to -5000 ppm, at roughly 30 to 33 kHz.
claims.source: TI application note SDAA423, USB 3.1 Gen 1 host TX electrical compliance, SSC parameters
claims.conditions: SuperSpeed signalling with SSC enabled; the depth is a range, not a single value
claims.note: Independent sources agree on triangular down-spread modulation at 30 to 33 kHz. The depth is specified as a RANGE of 0.4% to 0.5%, so "0 to -5000 ppm" describes the maximum excursion rather than the required one, and the page says so. USB 3.2 clause 6.5.3 is named as the normative source and has not been read.
claims.source_title: Texas Instruments SDAA423 — USB 3.1 Gen 1 host TX electrical compliance

claims.statement: USB 3.2 Gen 1 operates at 5 Gb/s.
claims.source: USB-IF, usb.org/usb-32-0
claims.conditions: Per lane, raw rate
claims.note: Public rate fact from the standards body. Says nothing about electrical requirements.
claims.source_title: USB-IF — USB 3.2 specification page

claims.statement: USB 3.2 Gen 2 operates at 10 Gb/s.
claims.source: USB-IF, usb.org/usb-32-0
claims.conditions: Per lane, raw rate
claims.note: Public rate fact from the standards body.
claims.source_title: USB-IF — USB 3.2 specification page

claims.statement: USB 3.2 Gen 2x2 operates at 20 Gb/s.
claims.source: USB-IF, usb.org/usb-32-0
claims.conditions: Two lanes, raw aggregate
claims.note: Public rate fact from the standards body. Two lanes, which is why it is split from Gen 2.
claims.source_title: USB-IF — USB 3.2 specification page

claims.statement: Controlled impedance is typically specified to +/-10%, with +/-7% available at a premium.
claims.source: fabricator capability statements, not a standard
claims.conditions: Varies by fabricator, stackup and volume
claims.note: Presented as typical fabricator capability rather than a specification.

claims.statement: The DC bias dependence of the same nominal MLCC part differs markedly between vendors, and X7R is not reliably less bias-sensitive than X5R.
claims.source: I. Novak, B. Williams, J. R. Miller, G. J. Blando, N. Shannon, 'DC and AC Bias Dependence of MLCC Capacitors and its Temperature Dependence', DesignCon East 2011
claims.conditions: 1 uF 0603 16 V parts from six vendors in X5R and X7R; DC stepped 0.2 V over -20 to +20 V; AC 10 mVrms and 500 mVrms
claims.note: Read from the paper's own conclusions, not from its plotted curves. The authors anonymise the vendors, which is why this site names no part's derating curve. This claim is the reason the panel takes the retained fraction as an input. Retrieved 12 September 2026 from the authors' paper archive. The link is http, not https: the https endpoint on that host returns 404, so an upgraded URL silently fails.
claims.source_title: Novak et al. — DC and AC Bias Dependence of MLCC Capacitors, DesignCon East 2011

claims.statement: MLCC DC bias sensitivity does not depend on temperature, so bias and temperature derating multiply as separable factors.
claims.source: Novak et al., DesignCon East 2011, conclusions
claims.conditions: Measured -5 degC to +70 degC. The same paper finds ESR DOES depend on temperature at high frequency and near the piezoelectric resonance, so the separability is a statement about capacitance only.
claims.note: This is what lets docs/real-capacitor-model.md carry bias and temperature in one retained scalar rather than a two-dimensional surface. Recorded because it is a measured finding being used as a modelling licence. Retrieved 12 September 2026 from the authors' paper archive. The link is http, not https: the https endpoint on that host returns 404, so an upgraded URL silently fails.
claims.source_title: Novak et al. — DC and AC Bias Dependence of MLCC Capacitors, DesignCon East 2011

claims.statement: Beyond the immediate capacitance change when DC bias is applied, MLCCs show a slower settling that can move capacitance by as much as a further 25% over a few minutes.
claims.source: Novak et al., DesignCon East 2011, conclusions
claims.conditions: Depends on dwell time and preconditioning; the paper treats measurement procedure as part of the result
claims.note: Quoted on the page as a reason the retained fraction is a band rather than a number. The figure is the paper's stated bound, not one read off a curve. Retrieved 12 September 2026 from the authors' paper archive. The link is http, not https: the https endpoint on that host returns 404, so an upgraded URL silently fails.
claims.source_title: Novak et al. — DC and AC Bias Dependence of MLCC Capacitors, DesignCon East 2011

claims.statement: A successive-approximation converter compares against its reference once per bit trial, so a reference that moves during a conversion weighs the early bits differently from the late ones.
claims.source: Analog Devices, "Voltage Reference Design for Precision Successive-Approximation ADCs"
claims.conditions: Charge-redistribution SAR with a single reference node; trial timing within one sample period
claims.note: States the mechanism directly: the reference is disturbed when the DAC inputs change, the DAC changes on each bit-test clock cycle, and the largest droop is at the MSB trial because that capacitor is the largest. That is exactly what this lab models. It describes charge-redistribution SAR parts; the lab’s trial TIMING within the sample period is a modelling choice and the page says so.
claims.source_title: Analog Devices — Voltage reference design for precision SAR ADCs

claims.statement: A one-bit delta-sigma modulator's feedback DAC is scaled by the reference, so reference ripple multiplies the bitstream rather than adding to the signal.
claims.source: Analog Devices sigma-delta ADC tutorial and AN-0979, on the one-bit feedback DAC and its reference
claims.conditions: Discrete-time, second order, one bit, single reference; not a continuous-time or multi-bit loop
claims.note: The one-bit feedback DAC switching between levels set by the reference is standard in the published descriptions of this topology, which is what makes reference ripple multiply the bitstream rather than add to the signal. Scoped rather than verified because the page now bounds the behaviour to the loop it simulates — discrete-time, second order, one bit — and says a continuous-time or multi-bit modulator will differ.
claims.source_title: Analog Devices — Sigma-delta ADC tutorial

claims.statement: Counting interference as noise, with the fundamental, DC and harmonics 2 to 6 excluded, is the usual convention for a converter dynamic test.
claims.source: Analog Devices MT-003 tutorial, "Understand SINAD, ENOB, SNR, THD, THD+N and SFDR"
claims.conditions: A coherent single-tone FFT test; exclusion widths depend on the window
claims.note: MT-003 defines SNR as the signal against all other spectral components below Nyquist EXCLUDING harmonics and DC, and SINAD as including harmonics but excluding DC. That is the convention this lab declares. The specific choices — harmonics 2 to 6, plus or minus 4 bins, Blackman-Harris — are this lab’s parameters, published in its result contract, not a standard’s requirement. IEEE Std 1241 has not been read and the page makes no compliance claim.
claims.source_title: Analog Devices MT-003 — Understand SINAD, ENOB, SNR, THD, THD+N and SFDR

claims.statement: Input-referred coupling appears as an offset error, a constant reference error as a gain error, and a reference that changes during the bit trials as a linearity error.
claims.source: Derived on this page from the converter model, and measured with it: offset 0.90 mV, gain −0.318 dBFS implying a 2.41 V effective reference, and THD rising to −53.5 dB
claims.conditions: Ideal SAR, shared converter clock so the disturbance repeats per conversion
claims.note: Narrowed in this batch: DNL and INL are named as the mechanism and explicitly not measured, because the lab runs no static ramp or histogram test and THD is not a substitute for one. The resemblance to a static nonlinearity holds only while the disturbance repeats in step with the conversions, which the page now says.

claims.statement: A sinc-cubed decimator is the usual filter after a second-order modulator, and it nulls exactly at multiples of the output data rate.
claims.source: Analog Devices AN-0979, "Digital Filtering Options", and the sigma-delta ADC tutorial
claims.conditions: Three cascaded length-OSR moving averages, decimating by OSR
claims.note: Better than "the usual choice": there is a stated design rule. The sinc order should be at least one more than the modulator order to keep out-of-band noise from aliasing back, which puts a second-order modulator at sinc-cubed, and the notch position follows the output data rate directly. Both halves of the claim, from the manufacturer’s own filter documentation.
claims.source_title: Analog Devices AN-0979 — Digital filtering options

claims.source: Isola 370HR Dk/Df tables, Revision C, 16 March 2020
claims.conditions: Typical values for this construction only; the table does not state its test method. Other constructions run from 3.63 (71 % resin) to 4.44 (41 % resin) at 100 MHz.
claims.note: Read from the primary table. The calculators offer this as the named mainstream FR-4 rather than an anonymous "FR-4", which no single source defines.
claims.source_title: Isola — 370HR Dk/Df tables

claims.conditions: The standard's timing definitions; says nothing about which bins a part or platform supports

claims.statement: The DDR5 DRAM has a 4-tap DFE on its DQ inputs; at 3200-6400 MT/s tap 1 spans -200 to +50 mV, tap 2 +/-75, tap 3 +/-60 and tap 4 +/-45 mV in 5 mV steps, with gain of +/-6 dB in 2 dB steps, and the stressed-eye test requires |t2| + |t3| + |t4| < 60 mV.
claims.source: Micron DDR5 SDRAM core data sheet, Rev. D 10/2022 (stated JESD79-5B compliant), Decision Feedback Equalization, tables 233 and 234, and the Rx stressed eye notes
claims.source_title: Micron — DDR5 SDRAM core data sheet (Rev. D, JESD79-5B compliant)
claims.conditions: 1X tap multiplier; 6800-8800 values are TBD in this revision
claims.note: Read from the data sheet. The data sheet notes these ranges are for relative evaluation and that absolute values are not production tested; the panel uses them as limits.

claims.statement: The DRAM receiver is tested with a stressed eye at the slicer, after the DFE: 95 mV by 0.25 UI at 3200 MT/s down to 57.5 mV by 0.23 UI at 6400, with the higher bins TBD in that revision.
claims.source: Micron DDR5 SDRAM core data sheet, Rev. D 10/2022 (stated JESD79-5B compliant), tables 321 and 322
claims.source_title: Micron — DDR5 SDRAM core data sheet (Rev. D, JESD79-5B compliant)
claims.conditions: Golden reference channel, with injected jitter and noise, BER 1e-16 by extrapolation from 1e-9
claims.note: The page states plainly that this is a receiver test condition, not a channel mask, and draws it only up to 6400.

claims.statement: DDR5's raw BER requirement is 1e-16 per lane in operation; receiver and transmitter limits are validated at 1e-9, needing 5.3e9 UI at 99.5% confidence.
claims.source: Micron DDR5 SDRAM core data sheet, Rev. D 10/2022 (stated JESD79-5B compliant), Minimum BER Requirements, table 277
claims.source_title: Micron — DDR5 SDRAM core data sheet (Rev. D, JESD79-5B compliant)
claims.conditions: Raw BER per lane, before correction
claims.note: The 5.3e9 figure is also derived on the page from -ln(0.005)/1e-9 and checked by check-numbers.py.

claims.statement: DDR5 modules route command, address and clock fly-by from the RCD, and data and strobes point to point; write leveling compensates the resulting CK-to-DQS skew at each DRAM, and DDR5 adds an internal cycle alignment step for the DRAM's unmatched internal path.
claims.source: Micron DDR5 SDRAM core data sheet, Rev. D 10/2022 (stated JESD79-5B compliant), Write Leveling Training Mode; Micron technical brief "DDR5: Key Module Features"
claims.source_title: Micron — DDR5 SDRAM core data sheet (Rev. D, JESD79-5B compliant)
claims.conditions: RDIMM; a UDIMM is fly-by from the controller
claims.note: The data sheet describes external leveling to the phase and cycle of CWL and the WICA internal alignment; the page's figure follows its description.

claims.statement: A DDR5 DIMM has two independent subchannels, each 32 data bits plus 8 for ECC on an ECC module; with burst length 16 one subchannel delivers 64 bytes.
claims.source: Micron technical brief "DDR5: Key Module Features"; Micron white paper "DDR5 SDRAM: New Features"
claims.source_title: Micron — DDR5: Key Module Features (technical brief)
claims.conditions: Standard modules; BL32 exists for x4 devices
claims.note: Both documents state the 40-bit subchannels and the BL16 to 64-byte relation.

claims.statement: DDR5 adds CS and CA training, internal write leveling, read training patterns including an LFSR pattern, a duty-cycle adjuster and a DQS interval oscillator; on-die ECC is single-error correction over 128 data and 8 parity bits; CRC covers reads as well as writes.
claims.source: Micron white papers "Introducing Micron DDR5 SDRAM" (table 1) and "DDR5 SDRAM: New Features"
claims.source_title: Micron — Introducing Micron DDR5 SDRAM: More Than a Generational Update
claims.conditions: Feature list
claims.note: Read from the comparison table and the RAS section.

claims.statement: On an RDIMM the host sends 7 CA pins per subchannel at double data rate to the RCD, which drives the DRAMs' 14 CA pins at single data rate; the DDR5 RDIMM edge has more VSS pins than DDR4's.
claims.source: Micron technical brief "DDR5: Key Module Features", table 1 and the CAI section
claims.source_title: Micron — DDR5: Key Module Features (technical brief)
claims.conditions: L/RDIMM
claims.note: The brief gives 2 x 7 DDR CA pins, a 14-pin SDR DRAM CA bus, and 127 VSS pins against 94.

claims.statement: The PMIC on a DDR5 module regulates the DRAM rails from a 12 V input on RDIMMs and 5 V on UDIMMs and SODIMMs.
claims.source: Micron technical brief "DDR5: Key Module Features" and white paper "DDR5: Client Module Features", pin tables
claims.source_title: Micron — DDR5: Client Module Features
claims.conditions: Bulk input pins
claims.note: Read from the two pin-difference tables.

claims.statement: DDR5 DRAMs terminate CA, CS and CK on die, and a CA_ODT strap selects group A (weak or off, typically for DRAMs along the chain) or group B (strong, 40 or 80 ohm, for the last DRAM of the fly-by).
claims.source: Micron white paper "DDR5: Client Module Features", DDR5 On-Die Termination; Micron DDR5 SDRAM core data sheet, Rev. D 10/2022 (stated JESD79-5B compliant), MR32/MR33
claims.source_title: Micron — DDR5: Client Module Features
claims.conditions: UDIMM/SODIMM description; RDIMMs also terminate on die
claims.note: The white paper gives the group A/B usage; the data sheet gives the CA ODT values.

claims.statement: DDR5 has 8 to 64 Gb device densities, a 16n prefetch, and doubles DDR4's bank groups.
claims.source: Micron white paper "Introducing Micron DDR5 SDRAM", table 1
claims.source_title: Micron — Introducing Micron DDR5 SDRAM: More Than a Generational Update
claims.conditions: As published in 2019; JESD79-5D's abstract covers 8 to 32 Gb devices
claims.note: Not stated on the page as numbers; kept so the comparison table's omissions are deliberate. The 64 Gb figure is the white paper's; JEDEC's current abstract says 8 to 32 Gb.

claims.statement: JEDEC's clocked UDIMM and SODIMM (JESD323, JESD324) add a clock driver that regenerates the clock on the module, presented as taking client modules from 6400 toward 7200 MT/s.
claims.source: EDN, "JEDEC unveils memory designs with DDR5 clock drivers", 17 October 2024, reporting JEDEC's announcement
claims.source_title: EDN — JEDEC unveils memory designs with DDR5 clock drivers
claims.conditions: Client modules; the CKD buffers clock only
claims.note: Reported announcement, not the standards. The page says the CKD regenerates the clock and that command and address still come from the controller.

claims.statement: Board makers' manuals name the slot to fill first with one DIMM per channel; ASUS's FAQ says DIMM_A2 and gives no reason.
claims.source: ASUS support FAQ 1049387, "How to install DRAM (memory) on motherboard"
claims.source_title: ASUS — How to install DRAM (memory) on motherboard
claims.conditions: Consumer boards; slot naming and routing are board specific
claims.note: The FAQ gives the slot, not the reason. The page offers the stub argument from its own model as a likely reason for a daisy-chained layout and tells the reader to follow the manual.

claims.statement: Server platforms commonly qualify a lower DDR5 data rate with two DIMMs per channel than with one.
claims.source: none read: platform memory population guides
claims.conditions: Platform dependent
claims.note: Stated on the page as common practice with the physical reason; no platform guide has been read for it.

claims.statement: LPDDR5X has a x16 channel per die, LVSTL I/O at a VDDQ of 0.5 V (0.45 V option, 0.3 V with ODT off), a differential WCK data clock at 2:1 or 4:1 to CK, an optional read strobe RDQS, and optional DRAM-side DFE and pre-emphasis advertised in mode registers.
claims.source: Micron 315b x32 Automotive LPDDR5X SDRAM data sheet, Rev. B 11/2022: features, and product-specific mode registers MR0 and MR24
claims.source_title: Micron — x32 Automotive LPDDR5X SDRAM data sheet (315b)
claims.conditions: One vendor family; DFE and pre-emphasis support vary by device
claims.note: Read from the features page and the mode register table: MR0 OP[6] pre-emphasis supported, OP[7] per-pin DFE not supported, MR24 OP[7] DFE supported (a 3-step DFE). The page says only that equalisation is optional and advertised per device.

claims.statement: JEDEC JESD318 (December 2023) defines CAMM2 modules for both DDR5 and LPDDR5/5X on a common connector with different pinouts, and aims LPDDR5/5X CAMM2s at notebooks and some server segments.
claims.source: JEDEC press release, "JEDEC Publishes New CAMM2 Memory Module Standard", 5 December 2023
claims.source_title: JEDEC — CAMM2 memory module standard announcement
claims.conditions: The announcement; the standard itself has not been read
claims.note: Read on jedec.org.
